ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Scissors — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces scissors through the card’s activity — cutting out simple shapes — with the grip, the rhythm and the safety rules that make cutting a victory lap, not a worry.

What is this?

Scissors are two sharp blades on two handles: one thumb up top, fingers below, and every open-close snips the paper between them. They are the strongest tool in the craft box.

What does it mean?

Cutting teaches cause and effect with a real machine: grip, squeeze, result. It also builds the hand arch strength that writing demands — cutting practice is writing practice in disguise.

What does the child need to know?

Child safety scissors (paper only), paper strips and shapes, and the two rules: paper only, and walking feet while holding them. Sitting down is the cutting position.

Why this matters

Cutting is a milestone skill teachers watch for, and it is the first tool that demands thumb-up orientation — the same position a pencil grip wants. Confidence with scissors opens every craft that follows.

What it teaches

Hand strength and arch control, bilateral coordination (both hands: one cuts, one holds the paper), snip rhythm, shape following, and the discipline of tool rules.

Words to learn

scissorssnipcutthumbopencloseshapescareful

Say this to your child

“"Scissors! Thumb on top — open... close... snip! Cut along the line... slowly... look, a square is coming out! Snips make shapes. What shape comes next?"”

Step by step

  1. Fit the hand: thumb in the small hole ON TOP, fingers in the big hole below.
  2. Practice the motion in the air — open... close... snip, snip.
  3. Cut a fat straight strip first: one confident snip at a time.
  4. Follow a drawn line around a big square — slow snips make smooth corners.
  5. Try the wavy snake line last, then sort the shapes: circle, square, snake.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, teal scissors stand open with blades up — the two handles show the thumb hole and the finger hole, the exact fit the lesson starts with.

Ask your child

"Where does the thumb go?" (small hole, on top) "What do scissors cut?" (paper — only paper) "Show me open and close." "What do we do when we carry scissors?" (walk, points down, or hand them over handles-first)

What your child can say or do

Your child may cut confetti until the whole floor sparkles, walk the house with scissors pointed down like a tiny professional, or cut one perfect circle and gasp at it — the gasp is mandatory.

Out in the real world

Barbers, tailors, doctors and paper mills all work with scissors or their bigger cousins — shears. Every haircut and every hem is the same open-close the child just learned, scaled up.

Try it together

Confetti factory: cut the day’s snippets into a jar, and when the jar is full, the confetti launches onto one glue-covered page — the mess becomes the mosaic, planned all week.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which finger goes on top?" (thumb) "What do we cut?" (paper) "Show me a snip." "Where do we walk with scissors?" (carefully — or we sit to cut)

This lesson pairs with the Scissors flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.
